Asymptotic behavior of a doubly haptotactic cross-diffusion model for oncolytic virotherapy

Yifu Wang, Chi Xu School of Mathematics and Statistics, Beijing Institute of Technology    Beijing 100081, P.R. China
Abstract

This paper considers a model for oncolytic virotherapy given by the doubly haptotactic cross-diffusion system

{ut=DuΔu−ξu∇⋅(u∇v)+μuu(1−u)−ρuz,vt=−(αu​u+αw​w)​v,wt=DwΔw−ξw∇⋅(w∇v)−w+ρuz,zt=Dz​Δ​z−δz​z−ρ​u​z+β​w,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=D_{u}\Delta u-\xi_{u}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\mu_{u}u(1-u)-\rho uz,\\ v_{t}=-(\alpha_{u}u+\alpha_{w}w)v,\\ w_{t}=D_{w}\Delta w-\xi_{w}\nabla\cdot(w\nabla v)-w+\rho uz,\\ z_{t}=D_{z}\Delta z-\delta_{z}z-\rho uz+\beta w,\end{array}\right.

with positive parameters Du,Dw,Dz,ξu,ξw,δz,ρD_{u},D_{w},D_{z},\xi_{u},\xi_{w},\delta_{z},\rho, αu,αw,μu,β\alpha_{u},\alpha_{w},\mu_{u},\beta. When posed under no-flux boundary conditions in a smoothly bounded domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, and along with initial conditions involving suitably regular data, the global existence of classical solution to this system was asserted in Tao and Winkler (2020). Based on the suitable quasi-Lyapunov functional, it is shown that when the virus replication rate β<1\beta<1, the global classical solution (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) is uniformly bounded and exponentially stabilizes to the constant equilibrium (1,0,0,0)(1,0,0,0) in the topology (L∞​(Ω))4(L^{\infty}(\Omega))^{4} as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty.

1 Introduction

As compared to the traditional treatment like chemotherapy or radiotherapy for cancer diseases, the prominent advantage of virotherapy is that the therapy can reduce the side-effect on the healthy tissue. In clinical treatments, the so-call oncolytic viruses (OV) which are either genetically engineered or naturally occurring can selectively attack the cancer cells and eventually destroy them without harming normal cells because virus can replicate inside the infected cells and proceed to infect adjacent cancer cells with the aim to drive the tumor cells to extinction ([8, 9]). Despite some partial success, implementation of virotherapy is not in sight. In fact, clinical data reveal that the efficacy of virotherapy will be reduced by many factors, such as circulating antibodies, various immune cells or even deposits of extracellular matrix may essentially decrease ([10, 16]). Therefore, to facilitate the understanding of the mechanisms that hinder virus spread, the authors of [1] proposed a mathematical model to describe the interaction between both uninfected and infected cancer cells, as well as extracellular matrix (ECM) and oncolytic virus particles, which is given by

{ut=DuΔu−ξu∇⋅(u∇v)+μuu(1−u)−ρuuz,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=−(αu​u+αw​w)​v+μv​v​(1−v),x∈Ω,t>0,wt=DwΔw−ξw∇⋅(w∇v)−δww+ρwuz,x∈Ω,t>0,zt=Dz​Δ​z−δz​z−ρz​u​z+β​w,x∈Ω,t>0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}u_{t}=D_{u}\Delta u-\xi_{u}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\mu_{u}u(1-u)-\rho_{u}uz,&&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ v_{t}=-(\alpha_{u}u+\alpha_{w}w)v+\mu_{v}v(1-v),&&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ w_{t}=D_{w}\Delta w-\xi_{w}\nabla\cdot(w\nabla v)-\delta_{w}w+\rho_{w}uz,&&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ z_{t}=D_{z}\Delta z-\delta_{z}z-\rho_{z}uz+\beta w,&&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\end{array}\right. (1.1)

in a smoothly bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, with positive parameters Du,Dw,Dz,ξu,ξw,αu,αwD_{u},D_{w},D_{z},\xi_{u},\xi_{w},\alpha_{u},\alpha_{w}, μu,δw,δz,β\mu_{u},\delta_{w},\delta_{z},\beta and nonnegative constants μv,ρu,ρw,ρz\mu_{v},\rho_{u},\rho_{w},\rho_{z}, and with the unknown variables u,w,zu,w,z and vv denoting the population densities of uninfected cancer cells, infected cancer cells, virus particles and ECM, respectively. Here the crucial modeling hypothesis underlying (1.1), which accounts for haptotactic motion of cancer cells and thereby marks a substantial difference between (1.1) and related more classical reaction-diffusion models for virus dynamics ([13, 19]), is that apart from its random diffusion, both uninfected and infected cancer cells bias their motion upward ECM gradients simultaneously due to the attraction by some macromolecules trapped in the ECM. In addition, the oncolytic virus particles infect the uninfected cancer cells upon contact with uninfected tumour cells, and new infectious virus particles are released at rate β>0\beta>0 when infected cells burst (a process known as lysis); beyond this, (1.1) presupposes that the ECM is degraded upon interacting with both type of cancer cells, and is possibly remodeled by the normal tissue according to logistic laws.

Due to its relevance in several biological contexts, inter alia the cancer invasion ([2, 5]), haptotaxis mechanism has received considerable attention in the analytical literature ([3, 11, 12, 14, 17, 21, 27, 28, 29, 30, 33, 32]). The most characteristic ingredient of the model (1.1) is the presence of two simultaneous haptotaxis processes of cancer cells, and thereby distinguishes it from most haptotaxis ([11, 29, 33]) and chemotaxis-haptotaxis systems ([3, 17, 27]) studied in the literature, especially the ECM is degraded by both type of cancer cells in (1.1) directly, rather matrix degrading enzymes (MDEs) secreted by tumor cells (see [12, 17, 18, 27] for example). It is observed that the former circumstance seems to widely restrict the accessibility to the approaches well established in the analysis of related reaction–diffusion systems, and accordingly the considerable challenges arise for the rigorous analysis of (1.1), particularly when addressing issues related to qualitative solution behaviour.

To the best of our knowledge, so far the quantitative comprehension available for (1.1) is yet mainly limited in some simple setting ([4, 15, 20, 23, 24, 22, 25, 26]). For instance, based on the construction of certain quasi–Lyapunov functional, Tao and Winkler ([22]) established the global classical solvability of (1.1) in the two-dimensional case. With respect to the boundedness of solutions to (1.1), authors in [15] considered some slightly more comprehensive variants of (1.1), which accounts for the haptotaxis mechanisms of both cancer cells and virions, in the situation when zero-order term has suitably strong degradation. Apart from that, existing analytical works indicate that the virus reproduction rate relative to the lysis rate of infected cancer cells appears to be critical in determining the large time behavior of the corresponding solutions at least in some simplified version of (1.1), inter alia upon neglecting haptotactic cross-diffusion of infected cancer cells and renew of ECM. Indeed, for the reaction–diffusion–taxis system

{ut=DuΔu−ξu∇⋅(u∇v)+μuu(1−u)−ρuz,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=−(αu​u+αw​w)​v,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=Dw​Δ​w−w+u​z,x∈Ω,t>0,zt=Dz​Δ​z−z−u​z+β​w,x∈Ω,t>0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}u_{t}=D_{u}\Delta u-\xi_{u}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\mu_{u}u(1-u)-\rho uz,&&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ v_{t}=-(\alpha_{u}u+\alpha_{w}w)v,&&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ w_{t}=D_{w}\Delta w-w+uz,&&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ z_{t}=D_{z}\Delta z-z-uz+\beta w,&&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\end{array}\right. (1.2)

it is shown in [24] that if β>1\beta>1, then for any reasonably regular initial data satisfying u0¯>1β−1\overline{u_{0}}>\frac{1}{\beta-1} the global classical solution of (1.2) with ρ=0,μu=0\rho=0,\mu_{u}=0 must blow up in infinite time, which is also implemented by the result on boundedness in the case when u0¯<1(β−1)+\overline{u_{0}}<\frac{1}{(\beta-1)_{+}} and v0≡0v_{0}\equiv 0 for any β>0\beta>0. Beyond the latter, it was proved that when ρ>0\rho>0 and μu=0\mu_{u}=0, the first solution component uu of (1.2) possesses a positive lower bounds whenever 0<β<10<\beta<1 and the initial data u0≢0u_{0}\not\equiv 0 ([25]). Furthermore, as a extension of above outcome, the asymptotic behavior of solution was investigated in [26] if 0<β<10<\beta<1. It is remarked that for system (1.2) with μu>0\mu_{u}>0 and 0<β<10<\beta<1, the convergence properties of the corresponding solutions was also discussed in [4]. We would like to mention that as the complementing results of [26], the recent paper [23] reveals that for any prescribed level γ∈(0,1(β−1)+)\gamma\in(0,\frac{1}{(\beta-1)_{+}}), the corresponding solution of (1.2) with μu=0,ρ≥0,β>0\mu_{u}=0,\rho\geq 0,\beta>0 will approach the constant equilibrium (u∞,0,0,0)(u_{\infty},0,0,0) asymptotically with some u∞>0u_{\infty}>0 whenever the initial deviation from homogeneous distribution (γ,0,0,0)(\gamma,0,0,0) is suitably small.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the dynamical features of the models involving the simultaneous haptotactic processes of both uninfected and infected cancer cells when the virus replication rate β<1\beta<1. To this end, we are concerned with the comprehensive haptotactic cross-diffusion systems of the form

{ut=DuΔu−ξu∇⋅(u∇v)+μuu(1−u)−ρuz,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=DwΔw−ξw∇⋅(w∇v)−w+ρuz,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=−(αu​u+αw​w)​v,x∈Ω,t>0,zt=Dz​Δ​z−δz​z−ρ​u​z+β​w,x∈Ω,t>0,(Du∇u−ξuu∇v)⋅ν=(Dw∇w−ξww∇v)⋅ν=∇z⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),z(x,0)=z0(x),x∈Ω\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=D_{u}\Delta u-\xi_{u}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\mu_{u}u(1-u)-\displaystyle\rho uz,&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{w_{t}=D_{w}\Delta w-\xi_{w}\nabla\cdot(w\nabla v)-w+\displaystyle\rho uz},&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{v_{t}=-(\alpha_{u}u+\alpha_{w}w)v},&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{z_{t}=D_{z}\Delta z-\delta_{z}z-\displaystyle\rho uz+\beta w},&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{(D_{u}\nabla u-\xi_{u}u\nabla v)\cdot\nu=(D_{w}\nabla w-\xi_{w}w\nabla v)\cdot\nu=\nabla z\cdot\nu=0},&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)},w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),z(x,0)=z_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega\end{array}\right. (1.3)

in a smoothly bounded domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}. To import the precise framework underlying the basic theory from [22] we shall henceforth assume that

{u0,w0,z0​and​v0​are nonnegative functions from​C2+ϑ​(Ω¯)​for some​ϑ∈(0,1),withu0≢0,w0≢0,z0≢0,v0≢0and∂w0∂ν=0on∂Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle{u_{0},w_{0},z_{0}~\hbox{and}\,v_{0}~\hbox{are nonnegative functions from}~C^{2+\vartheta}(\bar{\Omega})~\hbox{for some}~\vartheta\in(0,1),}\\ \displaystyle{\mbox{with}~u_{0}\not\equiv 0,~w_{0}\not\equiv 0,~z_{0}\not\equiv 0,~v_{0}\not\equiv 0~\hbox{and}~\frac{\partial w_{0}}{\partial\nu}=0~~\mbox{on}~~\partial\Omega.}\\ \end{array}\right. (1.4)

Hence the outcome of [22] asserts the global existence of a unique classical solution (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) to (1.3). Our main results reveal that whenever β<1\beta<1, (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) is uniformly bounded and exponentially converges to the constant equilibrium (1,0,0,0)(1,0,0,0) in the topology (L∞​(Ω))4(L^{\infty}(\Omega))^{4} in a large time limit, which can be stated as follows

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, Du,Dw,Dz,ξu,ξwD_{u},D_{w},D_{z},\xi_{u},\xi_{w}, μu,ρ,αu,αw,δz\mu_{u},\rho,\alpha_{u},\alpha_{w},\delta_{z} are positive parameters, and suppose that 0<β<10<\beta<1. Then system (1.3) admits a unique global classic positive solution satisfying

supt>0{‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖z⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)}<∞.\sup\limits_{t>0}\left\{\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|w(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|z(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\right\}<\infty. (1.5)

Moreover there exist positive constants η,ϱ,γ1\eta,\varrho,\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2} and C>0C>0 such that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−1‖L∞​(Ω)≤C​e−η​t,\|u(\cdot,t)-1\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\eta t}, (1.6)
‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤C​e−ϱ​t,\|w(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\varrho t}, (1.7)
‖z⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤C​e−γ1​t\|z(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\gamma_{1}t} (1.8)

as well as

‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤C​e−γ2​t.\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\gamma_{2}t}. (1.9)

Since the third equation in (1.3) is merely an ordinary differential equation, no smoothing action on the spatial regularity of vv can be expected. To overcome the analytical difficulties arising from the latter, inter alia in the derivation of global boundedness of solutions, we accordingly introduce the variable transformation a=e−χu​v​ua=e^{-\chi_{u}v}u and b=e−χw​v​wb=e^{-\chi_{w}v}w, and establish a priori estimate for the solution components a,ba,b of the corresponding equivalent system (2.2) below in the space L​l​o​g​L​(Ω)LlogL(\Omega) rather than the solution components u,wu,w to (1.3). Note that in the evolution of density vv of ECM fibers the quantity u,wu,w appears via a sink term, whereas it turns to a genuine superlinear production terms of system (2.2) in the style of χu​a​(αu​a​eχu​v+αw​b​eχw​v)​v\chi_{u}a(\alpha_{u}ae^{\chi_{u}v}+\alpha_{w}be^{\chi_{w}v})v and χw​b​(αu​a​eχu​v+αw​b​eχw​v)​v\chi_{w}b(\alpha_{u}ae^{\chi_{u}v}+\alpha_{w}be^{\chi_{w}v})v. Taking advantage of the exponential decay of ww in L1L^{1} norm in the case 0<β<10<\beta<1, we shall track the time evolution of

ℱ⁡(t)=∫Ωeχu​v​a​(⋅,t)​log⁡a⁡(⋅,t)+∫Ωeχw​v​b​(⋅,t)​log⁡b⁡(⋅,t)+∫Ωz2​(⋅,t)\mathcal{F}(t)=\int_{\Omega}e^{\chi_{u}v}a(\cdot,t)\log a(\cdot,t)+\int_{\Omega}e^{\chi_{w}v}b(\cdot,t)\log b(\cdot,t)+\int_{\Omega}z^{2}(\cdot,t)

with a=e−χu​v​ua=e^{-\chi_{u}v}u and b=e−χw​v​wb=e^{-\chi_{w}v}w, which is somewhat different from the quasi-Lyapunov functional (4.11) in [22] where a Dirichlet integral of v\sqrt{v} is involved. Here the quadratic degradation term in the first equation of (1.3) seems to be necessary. Thereafter applying a variant of the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality involving certain L​l​o​g​LLlogL-type norms and performing a Moser-type iteration, the L∞L^{\infty}-bounds of solutions is derived.

In addition, our result indicates that although haptotaxis mechanism may have some important influence on the properties of the related system on short or intermediate time scales, the large time behavior of solution to (1.3) can essentially be described by the corresponding haptotaxis-free system at least under the biological meaningful restriction β<1\beta<1. In order to prove Theorem 1.1, a first step is to derive a pointwise lower bound for a:=e−χu​v​ua:=e^{-\chi_{u}v}u (Lemma 4.2), which, in turn, amounts to establishing an exponential decay of zz with respect to the norm in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) (Lemma 4.2). To achieve the latter, we will make use of L1​(Ω)L^{1}(\Omega)-decay information of w,zw,z explicitly contained in Lemma 2.3. Scondly, as a consequence of the former, the exponential decay of vv with respect to L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) norm is achieved (Lemma 4.3), which along a a−1a^{-1}–testing procedure will provide quite weak convergence information of uu, inter alia the integrability property of ∇a\nabla\sqrt{a} in L2​((0,∞),L2​(Ω))L^{2}((0,\infty);L^{2}(\Omega)) (Lemma 4.4). The next step will consist of verifying the integrability of ∇v\nabla v in L2​((0,∞),L2​(Ω))L^{2}((0,\infty);L^{2}(\Omega)) rather than that of ata_{t} (Lemma 4.5), which will turn out to be sufficient a condition in the derivation of exponential decay property of ‖u⁡(⋅,t)−1‖Lp​(Ω)\|u(\cdot,t)-1\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}. Indeed, this integrability property of ∇v\nabla v enables us to derive an exponential decay of ∫Ω|∇v|2\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2} (Lemma 4.6), upon which and through a testing procedure, it is shown that the convergence property of uu actually takes place in the type of (4.22) (Lemma 4.7). Further, upon the above decay properties, we are able to verify that ∫Ω|∇v|4\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{4} decays exponentially by means of the suitable quasi-Lyapunov functional (Lemma 4.9). At this position, thanks to the integrability exponent in ∫Ω|∇v|4\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{4} exceeding the considered spatial dimension n=2n=2, the desired decay property stated in Theorem 1.1 can be exactly achieved.

This paper will be organized as follows: Section 2 will introduce an equivalent system of (1.3) and give out some basic priori estimates of classical solutions thereof, inter alia the weak decay properties of w,zw,z. Section 3 will focus on the construction of an entropy-type functional, which entails certain L​l​o​g​LLlogL-type norms and thereby allows us to establish the L∞L^{\infty}-bounds. Finally, starting from the exponential decay of quantities w,zw,z with respect to the norm in L1​(Ω)L^{1}(\Omega), we established the exponential convergence properties of the solutions in Section 4.

2 Preliminaries

Let us firstly recall the result in [22] which warrants the global smooth solvability of problem (1.3).

Lemma 2.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, Du,Dw,Dz,ξu,ξwD_{u},D_{w},D_{z},\xi_{u},\xi_{w}, μu,ρ,αu,αw,δz,β\mu_{u},\rho,\alpha_{u},\alpha_{w},\delta_{z},\beta are positive parameters. Then for any choice of (u0,v0,w0,z0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0},z_{0}) fulfilling (1.4), the problem (1.3) (1.4) possesses a uniquely determined classical solution (u,v,w,z)∈(C2,1​(Ω¯×[0,∞)))4(u,v,w,z)\in(C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty)))^{4} for which u>0,w>0,z>0u>0,w>0,z>0 and v≥0v\geq 0.

Following the variable of change used in related literature ([6, 15, 26, 28]), which can conveniently reformulate the haptotactic interaction in (1.3), we define χu:=ξuDu\chi_{u}:=\frac{\xi_{u}}{D_{u}} and χw:=ξwDw\chi_{w}:=\frac{\xi_{w}}{D_{w}} and set

a:=e−χu​v​u​and​b:=e−χw​v​w.a:=e^{-\chi_{u}v}u~~\hbox{and}~~b:=e^{-\chi_{w}v}w. (2.1)

Then we transform (1.3) into an equivalent system as below

{at=Due−χu​v∇⋅(eχu​v∇a)+f(a,b,v,c),x∈Ω,t>0,bt=Dwe−χw​v∇⋅(eχw​v∇b)+g(a,b,v,c),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=−(αu​a​eχu​v+αw​b​eχw​v)​v,x∈Ω,t>0,zt=Dz​Δ​z−δz​z−ρz​u​z+β​w,x∈Ω,t>0,∂a∂ν=∂b∂ν=∂z∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,a(x,0)=u0(x)e−χu​v0​(x),b(x,0)=w0(x)e−χw​v0​(x),x∈Ω,v0(x,0)=v0(x),z(x,0)=z0(x),x∈Ω\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}a_{t}=D_{u}e^{-\chi_{u}v}\nabla\cdot(e^{\chi_{u}v}\nabla a)+f(a,b,v,c),&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ b_{t}=D_{w}e^{-\chi_{w}v}\nabla\cdot(e^{\chi_{w}v}\nabla b)+g(a,b,v,c),&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ v_{t}=-(\alpha_{u}ae^{\chi_{u}v}+\alpha_{w}be^{\chi_{w}v})v,&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ z_{t}=D_{z}\Delta z-\delta_{z}z-\rho_{z}uz+\beta w,&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial a}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial b}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial\nu}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ a(x,0)=u_{0}(x)e^{-\chi_{u}v_{0}(x)},~b(x,0)=w_{0}(x)e^{-\chi_{w}v_{0}(x)},&x\in\Omega,\\ v_{0}(x,0)=v_{0}(x),~~z(x,0)=z_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega\end{array}\right. (2.2)

with

f⁡(a,b,v,c):=μu​a​(1−a​eχu​v)−ρ​a​z+χu​a​(αu​a​eχu​v+αw​b​eχw​v)​v,f(a,b,v,c):=\mu_{u}a(1-ae^{\chi_{u}v})-\displaystyle\rho az+\chi_{u}a(\alpha_{u}ae^{\chi_{u}v}+\alpha_{w}be^{\chi_{w}v})v,

as well as

g⁡(a,b,v,c):=−b+ρ​a​z​e(χu−χw)​v+χw​b​(αu​a​eχu​v+αw​b​eχw​v)​v.g(a,b,v,c):=-b+\displaystyle\rho aze^{(\chi_{u}-\chi_{w})v}+\chi_{w}b(\alpha_{u}ae^{\chi_{u}v}+\alpha_{w}be^{\chi_{w}v})v.

In our subsequent analysis, unless otherwise stated we shall assume that (a,v,b,z)(a,v,b,z) is the global classical solution to (2.2) addressed in Lemma 2.1.

The damping effects of quadratic degradation in the first equation in (1.3) will be important for us to verify the global boundedness of the solutions. Let we first apply straightforward argument to achieve the following basic L1L^{1}-bounds for u,wu,w and zz, which is also valid for the solution components a,ba,b of (2.2).

Lemma 2.2.

For all t>0t>0, the solution (u,w,v,z)(u,w,v,z) satisfies

∫Ωu⁡(⋅,t)≤max⁡{∫Ωu0,|Ω|}:=mu,\int_{\Omega}u(\cdot,t)\leq\max\left\{\int_{\Omega}u_{0},|\Omega|\right\}:=m_{u}, (2.3)

and

v≤‖v0‖L∞​(Ω):=mvv\leq\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}:=m_{v} (2.4)

and

∫Ωw⁡(⋅,t)≤max⁡{‖u0‖L1​(Ω)+‖w0‖L1​(Ω),|Ω|​μumin⁡{1,μu}}:=mw,\int_{\Omega}w(\cdot,t)\leq\max\left\{\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}+\|w_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)},\frac{|\Omega|\mu_{u}}{\min\{1,\mu_{u}\}}\right\}:=m_{w}, (2.5)

as well as

∫Ωz⁡(⋅,t)≤max⁡{∫Ωz0,β​mwδz}:=mz.\int_{\Omega}z(\cdot,t)\leq\max\left\{\int_{\Omega}z_{0},\frac{\beta m_{w}}{\delta_{z}}\right\}:=m_{z}. (2.6)
Proof.

It is easy to see that (2.3) can be derived through an integration of the first equation in (1.3) along with Cauchy–Schwarz’s inequality, and (2.4) is a direct consequence of (αu​u+αw​w)​v≥0(\alpha_{u}u+\alpha_{w}w)v\geq 0 due to the nonnegativity of u,wu,w and vv.

In addition, integrating the ww-equation as well as uu-equation respectively and adding the corresponding results, we then have

dd​t​(∫Ωu+∫Ωw)+∫Ωw+μu​∫Ωu≤|Ω|​μu,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\int_{\Omega}u+\int_{\Omega}w\right)+\int_{\Omega}w+\mu_{u}\int_{\Omega}u\leq|\Omega|\mu_{u}, (2.7)

which readily leads to (2.5) upon an ODE comparison. At last, thanks to (2.5), (2.6) clearly results from the integration of zz-equation in (1.3). ∎

∫Ωa⁡(⋅,t)​|log⁡a⁡(⋅,t)|≤∫Ωeχu​v​a​(⋅,t)​log⁡a⁡(⋅,t)−2​∫a<1eχu​v​a​(⋅,t)​log⁡a⁡(⋅,t)≤∫Ωeχu​v​a​(⋅,t)​log⁡a⁡(⋅,t)+2​|Ω|​eχu​mve.\begin{array}[]{rl}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}a(\cdot,t)|\log a(\cdot,t)|&\leq\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}e^{\chi_{u}v}a(\cdot,t)\log a(\cdot,t)-2\int_{a<1}e^{\chi_{u}v}a(\cdot,t)\log a(\cdot,t)\\[5.69054pt] &\leq\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}e^{\chi_{u}v}a(\cdot,t)\log a(\cdot,t)+\frac{2|\Omega|e^{\chi_{u}m_{v}}}{e}.\end{array}

Likewise, we can also obtain

According to (3.8), there exits c1>0c_{1}>0 such that

with c2=2​|Ω|e​(eχw​mv+eχu​mv)+c1c_{2}=\frac{2|\Omega|}{e}(e^{\chi_{w}m_{v}}+e^{\chi_{u}m_{v}})+c_{1} for all t>t0t>t_{0}, and thus complete the proof. ∎

The a priori estimates for a,ba,b gained in Lemma 3.4 is the cornerstone to establish a L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega)-bound for solution (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z). Indeed, one can proceed to derive obtain L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega)-bound by means of some quite straightforward LpL^{p} testing procedures.

4 Asymptotic behavior

On the basis of the exponential decay of quantities w,zw,z with respect to the norm in L1​(Ω)L^{1}(\Omega) and global boundedness of solutions, we will address the large time asymptotics of the solution (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) to (1.3). To this end, we first turn the L1L^{1}-decay information explicitly contained in Lemma 2.3 to the decay property of zz in L∞L^{\infty}-norm by an appropriate application of the parabolic smoothing estimates in the two-dimensional domain.

Lemma 4.1.

Let (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) be the global solutions of (1.3) with β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1). Then for all t>0t>0, we have

z⁡(⋅,t)=et⁡(Dz​Δ−δz)​z0+∫0te(t−s)​(Dz​Δ−δz)​(β​w−ρ​u​z)​(⋅,s)​𝑑s≤et⁡(Dz​Δ−δz)​z0+β​∫0te(t−s)​(Dz​Δ−δz)​w​(⋅,s)​𝑑s≤e−δz​t​‖z0‖L∞​(Ω)+β​c3​∫0t(1+(t−s)−12)​e−δz​(t−s)​‖w⁡(⋅,s)‖L2​(Ω)​𝑑s≤e−δz​t​‖z0‖L∞​(Ω)+β​c2​c3​∫0t(1+(t−s)−12)​e−δz​(t−s)​e−δ​s2​𝑑s≤e−δz​t∥z0∥L∞​(Ω)+βc2c3c4e−min{δz,δ2)t\begin{array}[]{rl}z(\cdot,t)&=e^{t(D_{z}\Delta-\delta_{z})}z_{0}+\displaystyle\int^{t}_{0}e^{(t-s)(D_{z}\Delta-\delta_{z})}(\beta w-\rho uz)(\cdot,s)ds\\ &\leq e^{t(D_{z}\Delta-\delta_{z})}z_{0}+\beta\displaystyle\int^{t}_{0}e^{(t-s)(D_{z}\Delta-\delta_{z})}w(\cdot,s)ds\\ &\leq\displaystyle e^{-\delta_{z}t}\|z_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\beta c_{3}\int^{t}_{0}(1+(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\delta_{z}(t-s)}\|w(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}ds\\ &\leq\displaystyle e^{-\delta_{z}t}\|z_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\beta c_{2}c_{3}\int^{t}_{0}(1+(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\delta_{z}(t-s)}e^{-\frac{\delta s}{2}}ds\\ &\leq\displaystyle e^{-\delta_{z}t}\|z_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\beta c_{2}c_{3}c_{4}e^{-min\{\delta_{z},\frac{\delta}{2})t}\end{array} (4.4)

with some c4>0c_{4}>0, which along with the nonnegativity of zz entails that (4.1) holds with C=‖z0‖L∞​(Ω)+β​c2​c3​c4.C=\|z_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\beta c_{2}c_{3}c_{4}. ∎

Now thanks to the uniform decay property of zz, a pointwise lower bound for a=u​e−χu​va=ue^{-\chi_{u}v} can be achieved by means of an argument based on comparison with spatially flat functions, which is documented as follows.

Lemma 4.3.

Lemma 4.5.

Let the assumption of Lemma 4.1 hold. Then we have

Proof.

=2​ρ​∫Ωa​b​z​eχw​v+2​χw​∫Ωeχw​v​b2​(αu​a​eχu​v+αw​b​eχw​v)​v,\displaystyle=2\rho\int_{\Omega}abze^{\chi_{w}v}+2\chi_{w}\int_{\Omega}e^{\chi_{w}v}b^{2}(\alpha_{u}ae^{\chi_{u}v}+\alpha_{w}be^{\chi_{w}v})v,

Now since

Beyond the integrability of ∫Ω|∇v|2\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2} over (0,∞)(0,\infty), we make use of the explicit expression of ∇v\nabla v together with (4.17) and (4.12) to identify that ∫Ω|∇v|2\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2} exponentially decays.

Lemma 4.6.

(4.20)

at=Du△a+Du∇v⋅∇a+f(x,t),x∈Ω,t>0a_{t}=D_{u}\triangle a+D_{u}\nabla v\cdot\nabla a+f(x,t),\quad x\in\Omega,\quad t>0

and

as well as

Likely, we can get

dd​t​‖∇b‖L2​(Ω)2+Dw2​c2​‖∇b‖L2​(Ω)2+Dw4​‖△​b‖L2​(Ω)2≤4​Dw​χw4​c1​c32​‖∇v‖L4​(Ω)4+2Dw​‖g‖L2​(Ω)2.\begin{array}[]{rl}&\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\|\nabla b\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\frac{D_{w}}{2c_{2}}\|\nabla b\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\displaystyle\frac{D_{w}}{4}\|\triangle b\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\\[8.53581pt] \leq&\displaystyle 4D_{w}\chi_{w}^{4}c_{1}c_{3}^{2}\|\nabla v\|^{4}_{L^{4}(\Omega)}+\frac{2}{D_{w}}\|g\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}.\end{array} (4.35)

with g⁡(x,t)=−b+ρ​u​e−χw​v​z+χw​b​(αu​u+αw​w)​vg(x,t)=-b+\displaystyle\rho ue^{-\chi_{w}v}z+\chi_{w}b(\alpha_{u}u+\alpha_{w}w)v.

Now in order to appropriately compensate the first summand on right-hand side of (4.34) and (4.35), we use the third equation in (2.2) to see that

14​dd​t​∫Ω|∇v|4=−∫Ω|∇v|2∇v⋅∇vt=−αu∫Ωa(v+χu)eχu​v|∇v|4−αu∫Ωveχu​v|∇v|2∇v⋅∇a−αw∫Ωb(v+χw)eχw​v|∇v|4−αw∫Ωveχw​v|∇v|2∇v⋅∇b.\begin{array}[]{rl}&\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{4}\\ =&-\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2}\nabla v\cdot\nabla v_{t}\\ =&-\alpha_{u}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}a(v+\chi_{u})e^{\chi_{u}v}|\nabla v|^{4}-\alpha_{u}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}ve^{\chi_{u}v}|\nabla v|^{2}\nabla v\cdot\nabla a\\ &-\alpha_{w}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}b(v+\chi_{w})e^{\chi_{w}v}|\nabla v|^{4}-\alpha_{w}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}ve^{\chi_{w}v}|\nabla v|^{2}\nabla v\cdot\nabla b.\end{array} (4.36)

Here recalling the uniform positivity of aa stated in Lemma 4.2, we can pick c4>0c_{4}>0 fulfilling

αu​∫Ωa⁡(v+χu)​eχu​v​|∇v|4≥αu​χu​c4​∫Ω|∇v|4\alpha_{u}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}a(v+\chi_{u})e^{\chi_{u}v}|\nabla v|^{4}\geq\alpha_{u}\chi_{u}c_{4}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{4}

and thus infer by the Young inequality and Lemma 2.2 that for all t>t0t>t_{0}

dd​t​∫Ω|∇v|4+c5​∫Ω|∇v|4≤c6​‖v⁡(⋅,t0)‖L∞​(Ω)​∫Ω(|∇a|4+|∇b|4)\begin{array}[]{rl}&\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{4}+c_{5}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{4}\\ \leq&c_{6}\|v(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}(|\nabla a|^{4}+|\nabla b|^{4})\end{array} (4.37)

with constants c5>0c_{5}>0, c6>0c_{6}>0.

Now if we write d1:=8​c1​c32​(Du​χu4+Dw​χw4)c5d_{1}:=\frac{8c_{1}c_{3}^{2}(D_{u}\chi_{u}^{4}+D_{w}\chi_{w}^{4})}{c_{5}}, combining (4.37), (4.34) with (4.35) yields

dd​t​(‖∇a‖L2​(Ω)2+‖∇b‖L2​(Ω)2+d1​‖∇v‖L4​(Ω)4)+Du2​c2​‖∇a‖L2​(Ω)2+Du4​‖△​a‖L2​(Ω)2+Dw2​c2​‖∇b‖L2​(Ω)2+Dw4​‖△​b‖L2​(Ω)2+c5​d12​‖∇v‖L4​(Ω)4≤c6​d1​‖v⁡(⋅,t0)‖L∞​(Ω)​(‖∇a‖L4​(Ω)4+‖∇b‖L4​(Ω)4)+2Du​‖f‖L2​(Ω)2+2Dw​‖g‖L2​(Ω)2,\begin{array}[]{rl}&\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\left(\|\nabla a\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\|\nabla b\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+d_{1}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4}\right)\\[8.53581pt] &+\displaystyle\frac{D_{u}}{2c_{2}}\|\nabla a\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\displaystyle\frac{D_{u}}{4}\|\triangle a\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\frac{D_{w}}{2c_{2}}\|\nabla b\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\displaystyle\frac{D_{w}}{4}\|\triangle b\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\frac{c_{5}d_{1}}{2}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4}\\[8.53581pt] \leq&c_{6}d_{1}\|v(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}(\|\nabla a\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4}+\|\nabla b\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4})+\displaystyle\frac{2}{D_{u}}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\frac{2}{D_{w}}\|g\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2},\end{array} (4.38)

which together with (4.31), (4.32) and Lemma 4.3 entails that there exists t1>1t_{1}>1 suitably large such that for all t>t1t>t_{1},

dd​t​(‖∇a‖L2​(Ω)2+‖∇b‖L2​(Ω)2+d1​‖∇v‖L4​(Ω)4)+Du2​c2​‖∇a‖L2​(Ω)2+Dw2​c2​‖∇b‖L2​(Ω)2+c5​d12​‖∇v‖L4​(Ω)4≤2Du​‖f‖L2​(Ω)2+2Dw​‖g‖L2​(Ω)2.\begin{array}[]{rl}&\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\left(\|\nabla a\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\|\nabla b\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+d_{1}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4}\right)\\[8.53581pt] &+\displaystyle\frac{D_{u}}{2c_{2}}\|\nabla a\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\frac{D_{w}}{2c_{2}}\|\nabla b\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\frac{c_{5}d_{1}}{2}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4}\\[8.53581pt] \leq&\displaystyle\frac{2}{D_{u}}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\frac{2}{D_{w}}\|g\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}.\end{array} (4.39)

Due to Lemma 3.5, we see that

|f⁡(x,t)|2+|g⁡(x,t)|2≤c7​(|u⁡(x,t)−1|2+|w⁡(x,t)|2+|z⁡(x,t)|2+|v⁡(x,t)|2)|f(x,t)|^{2}+|g(x,t)|^{2}\leq c_{7}(|u(x,t)-1|^{2}+|w(x,t)|^{2}+|z(x,t)|^{2}+|v(x,t)|^{2})

with some c7>0c_{7}>0, and thus there exist η3>0\eta_{3}>0 and c8>0c_{8}>0 such that

∫Ω|f⁡(x,t)|2+|g⁡(x,t)|2≤c8​e−η3​t​for all t>t1,\int_{\Omega}|f(x,t)|^{2}+|g(x,t)|^{2}\leq c_{8}e^{-\eta_{3}t}~~\hbox{for all $t>t_{1},$} (4.40)

thanks to Lemma 4.7, Lemma 4.8, Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 4.3. Therefore (4.29) readily results from (4.40) and (4.39). ∎

At this position, as an application of known smoothing estimates for the Neumann heat semigroup, the latter readily turns to the exponential decay property of u−1u-1 as well as ww with respect to L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega)-norm.

Lemma 4.10.

Let the conditions in Theorem 1.1 hold. Then there exist η,ϱ>0\eta,\varrho>0 and C>0C>0 fulfilling

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−1‖L∞​(Ω)≤C​e−η​t\|u(\cdot,t)-1\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\eta t} (4.41)

as well as

‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤C​e−ϱ​t\|w(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\varrho t} (4.42)

for all t>0t>0.

Proof.

Since the proof is similar to that of Lemma 4.7, we only give a short proof of (4.41). In view to known smoothing estimates for the Neumann heat semigroup on Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} ([31]), there exist c1>0c_{1}>0, c2>0c_{2}>0 fulfilling

‖eσ​Du​Δ​φ‖L∞​(Ω)≤c1​σ−12​‖φ‖L2​(Ω)\left\|e^{\sigma D_{u}\Delta}\varphi\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq c_{1}\sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)} (4.43)

for each φ∈C0​(Ω)\varphi\in C^{0}(\Omega), and for all φ∈(L4​(Ω))2\varphi\in\left(L^{4}\left(\Omega\right)\right)^{2},

‖eσ​Du​Δ∇⋅φ‖L∞​(Ω)≤c2(1+σ−34)e−λ1​σ‖φ‖L4​(Ω)\left\|e^{\sigma D_{u}\Delta}\nabla\cdot\varphi\right\|_{L^{\infty}\left(\Omega\right)}\leq c_{2}(1+\sigma^{-\frac{3}{4}})e^{-\lambda_{1}\sigma}\left\|\varphi\right\|_{L^{4}\left(\Omega\right)} (4.44)

with λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 the first nonzero eigenvalue of −Δ-\Delta in Ω\Omega under the Neumann boundary condition.

According to the variation-of-constants representation of uu related to the the first equation in (1.3), we utilize (4.43) and (4.44) to infer that

‖(u−1)​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤∥et⁡(Du​Δ−1)(u0−1)∥L∞​(Ω)+ξu∫t0∥e(t−s)​(Du​Δ−1)∇⋅(u∇v)∥L∞​(Ω)ds+∫t0∥e(t−s)​(Du​Δ−1)((μuu−1)(1−u)−ρuz)∥L∞​(Ω)ds≤e−t​‖u0−1‖L∞​(Ω)+c3​∫0t(1+(t−s)−34)​e−(1+λ1)​(t−s)​‖∇v​(⋅,s)‖L4​(Ω)​𝑑s+c3∫t0(1+(t−s)−12)e−(t−s)(∥(u−1)(⋅,s)∥L2​(Ω)+∥z(⋅,s)∥L2​(Ω))ds\begin{array}[]{rl}&\|(u-1)(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\\ \leq&\|e^{t(D_{u}\Delta-1)}(u_{0}-1)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\xi_{u}\displaystyle\int^{t}_{0}\|e^{(t-s)(D_{u}\Delta-1)}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}ds\\ &+\displaystyle\int^{t}_{0}\|e^{(t-s)(D_{u}\Delta-1)}((\mu_{u}u-1)(1-u)-\rho uz)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}ds\\ \leq&\displaystyle e^{-t}\|u_{0}-1\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+c_{3}\int^{t}_{0}(1+(t-s)^{-\frac{3}{4}})e^{-(1+\lambda_{1})(t-s)}\|\nabla v(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}ds\\ &+c_{3}\displaystyle\int^{t}_{0}(1+(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}})e^{-(t-s)}(\|(u-1)(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\|z(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)})ds\end{array} (4.45)

with some c3>0c_{3}>0. This readily establish (4.41) with appropriate η>0\eta>0 in view of (4.29), (4.22) and (4.1). ∎

Thereby our main result has essentially been proved already.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.  The statement on global boundedness of classical solutions has been asserted by Lemma 3.5. The convergence properties in (1.6)–(1.9) are precisely established by Lemma 4.10, Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 4.3, respectively.
